The Supreme Court of South Carolina
Re: Fees for Copying and Other Related Services
Appellate Case No. 2016-002381
ORDER
This order establishes the fees to be charged by the Supreme Court of South
Carolina and the offices, commissions, and boards of the South Carolina Judicial
Branch (SCJB) (including the Office of Court Administration, the Office of Fiscal
Services, the Office of Human Resources, the Office of Information Technology,
the Office of Disciplinary Counsel, the Commission on Lawyer Conduct, and the
Commission on Judicial Conduct), and by the South Carolina Court of Appeals for
providing copies of documents and other related services.
(1) Copying Fee.
Photocopies shall be made by SCJB staff, and a fee of $0.25 per page will be
charged.
For physical photocopies of documents in bound records and on microfilm, a fee
of $0.25 per page plus the time spent by SCJB staff to obtain and produce the
copies will be charged at the rate provided in section 5.
For digital copies of documents, including those in bound records and on
microfilm, and document requests that are too large to be emailed, a fee of $20.00
per digital media (e.g., a USB flash drive) plus the time spent by SCJB staff to
obtain and produce the copies will be charged as per section 5.
(2) Mailing Fee.
For mailing copies of documents, the actual cost of mailing through the United
States Postal Service (USPS), FedEx, UPS, or other provider will be charged and
1

must be paid in advance by the requestor.
(3) Certified Copies.
In addition to the cost of copying the document, a fee of $2.00 per page will be
charged for providing a certified copy of a document filed with the Supreme Court
of South Carolina or the South Carolina Court of Appeals, up to a maximum fee
of $50.00.
(4) Oral Arguments.
Live transmission of oral arguments of the Supreme Court of South Carolina and
the South Carolina Court of Appeals is available for viewing at no charge on the
website for the SCJB. Previously held oral arguments are archived on the website
and are also available for viewing at no charge. An audio copy of oral arguments
available on the website may be obtained on physical transfer media (such as a
USB flash drive) provided by the SCJB at a cost of $20.00. For oral arguments
that are not available in the court's archive access, an audio copy, if available, may
be obtained on physical transfer media provided by the court at a cost of $20.00.
(5) Search and Preparation Fees.
No fee will be charged for searching for and preparing a document if the service is
completed within fifteen minutes. If the service requires more than fifteen
minutes, the requestor will be billed for the time after the initial free minutes at a
rate of $20.00 per hour.
(6) Payment of Costs.
All fees required by this order shall be paid in cash, or by check or money order
made payable to the South Carolina Judicial Branch. Further, the fees shall
generally be paid in advance by the requestor. The custodian of the record may
also require a deposit to be filed before searching for a record.
If the request is from a corporation, partnership, law firm, or other business entity,
the custodian of the records may allow the requestor to be billed for the fees. If
the requestor is billed and fails to pay within thirty days of the date of the bill,
further requests from that requestor will not be honored until the account is paid
2

in full. A requestor who fails to pay a bill within sixty days of the date of the bill
will lose the ability to be billed for charges for a period of one year.
(7) Bulk Distribution of and Compiled Information from Bulk Records.
Requests regarding bulk records are governed by Rule 610, SCACR, and not this
order.
(8) Waiver of Costs.
Any request to waive or reduce the fees provided by this order shall be decided by
the custodian of the record involved. As a general rule, the fee will not be waived
or reduced unless the custodian determines that furnishing the information
without charge or a reduced charge would be in the public interest because
furnishing the information can be considered as primarily benefiting the general
public. Members of the South Carolina General Assembly may receive copies of
records and documents at no charge when their request relates to their legislative
duties. See S.C. Code Ann. § 30-4-30(b) (2007 & Supp. 2025).
(9) Effective Date.
This order is effective immediately upon signing, and the order shall apply to all
requests for copying or other services received on or after the date of this order.
IT IS SO ORDERED.

PER CURIAM: In this attorney disciplinary matter, Respondent and the Office
of Disciplinary Counsel (ODC) have entered into an Agreement for Discipline by
Consent pursuant to Rule 21 of the Rules for Lawyer Disciplinary Enforcement
(RLDE) contained in Rule 413 of the South Carolina Appellate Court Rules
(SCACR). In the Agreement, Respondent admits misconduct, agrees to pay costs,
and consents to the imposition of a confidential admonition or a public reprimand.
We accept the Agreement and issue a public reprimand.
I.
Respondent was admitted to practice in 1979 and has no prior disciplinary history.
This Agreement resolves two pending matters concerning the same facts and
circumstances, which are addressed collectively below.
11

On December 7, 2018, Respondent was assigned by an auto insurance carrier to
defend a personal injury lawsuit filed on November 15, 2018, against an insured
motorist. Respondent requested an extension by email to file an answer but sent it
to the wrong email address and never followed up with the plaintiff's counsel
regarding the extension request. The plaintiff's law firm emailed Respondent on
December 12, 2018, about scheduling a deposition of Respondent's client, but
Respondent did not respond. The plaintiff's firm also called Respondent's office on
December 13, 2018, and left a voicemail, but Respondent did not respond.
Respondent did not file an answer to the complaint. Respondent admits he failed
to properly calendar the deadline. On March 27, 2019, the plaintiff filed a motion
for default, and an order of default was entered against Respondent's client.
Respondent learned of his error when the motion for default was filed. Respondent
notified his malpractice carrier, and on April 4, 2019, Respondent filed a motion
for relief from the entry of default under Rule 55(c), SCRCP.1
On April 24, 2019, Respondent received notice that a deposition of a medical
expert would be held May 7, 2019. Respondent did not attend the deposition. In
July 2019, Respondent missed another deposition of a second medical expert, for
which he received proper notice.
Sometime after Respondent filed his motion for relief from default but before the
hearing, Respondent met with the client to discuss the status of the case and the
consequences for the client having a judgment against him. Respondent and the
client discussed the client's assets and the exemptions available to him under the
law. Respondent represents it was clear to him that the client had no assets above
the exemption limits. Respondent advised the client that he believed the plaintiff
would likely seek an assignment of the client's malpractice claim against
Respondent and/or the insurance company.
At a second meeting with the client on August 5, 2019, Respondent and the client
discussed entering an agreement to settle the client's potential malpractice claim
against Respondent and the insurance company. Respondent told the client orally
that the client would need independent legal advice. However, Respondent did not
provide the client with this advice in writing. The client told Respondent that he

JUSTICE HILL: Anderson resident Reid Fleming alleges he was burned when the
model 18650 lithium-ion battery in his vape pen exploded. His injury occurred in
Charleston. Fleming claims LG Chem, Ltd. (LG) manufactured the battery, which
he bought in Charleston from The Planet Vape, LLC. Fleming sued LG, Planet
Vape, and others in South Carolina circuit court for his injuries. LG moved to
dismiss Fleming's claim against it, contending South Carolina lacked personal
jurisdiction. The trial court granted LG's motion, and the court of appeals affirmed,
with Judge Hewitt dissenting. Fleming v. Planet Vape, LLC, Op. No. 2025-UP-295
(S.C. Ct. App. filed August 13, 2025).
We granted Fleming's petition for writ of certiorari to consider whether due process
permits LG to be subject to personal jurisdiction in South Carolina under the
circumstances here. We hold it does.
I. Fleming's Complaint
LG is a South Korean corporation with its principal offices located in Seoul. Its
consumer electronics business spans the globe. In his complaint, Fleming alleges
LG has numerous contacts with South Carolina. According to Fleming, these
contacts relate to his claims because LG manufactures lithium-ion batteries knowing
they will be distributed and sold in South Carolina to individuals who will use them
to power vape pens. Despite this knowledge, LG has done "virtually nothing to
prevent its lithium-ion battery products from being sold individually throughout the
United States and, specifically, in South Carolina." Fleming claims LG continued
this distribution scheme knowing vaping devices in which its lithium-ion batteries
were being used lack adequate circuitry and other safety protections. He further
alleges LG knows its lithium-ion batteries are being rewrapped by its commercial
customers and being sold throughout the United States and online for individual use.
Fleming's complaint listed five cases pending in South Carolina where the circuit
court has exercised personal jurisdiction over LG in similar lawsuits involving
individuals injured by LG lithium-ion batteries used to power vape pens. He also
contends LG has consented to personal jurisdiction in a federal court action in South
Carolina involving an exploding lithium-ion battery.
16

II. Personal Jurisdiction: The Long Arm Statute and Due Process
A court may only exert its jurisdictional power when that power has been
legislatively granted and does not exceed constitutional limits. Accordingly,
determining whether a South Carolina court has personal jurisdiction over a non-
resident defendant involves two inquiries. S. Plastics Co. v. S. Com. Bank, 310 S.C.
256, 259, 423 S.E.2d 128, 130 (1992). The first inquiry—which asks whether the
jurisdictional reach of our long-arm statute extends to the defendant's conduct—is
not at issue here. The second inquiry asks if exercising personal jurisdiction over
the defendant comports with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
See U.S. Const. amend. XIV. This is the familiar world still governed by the
landmark decision in International Shoe, which held that due process allows a court
to exercise personal jurisdiction over a non-resident defendant when the defendant
has enough "minimum contacts" with the forum state to make the state's jurisdiction
reasonable in the sense that it "does not offend 'traditional notions of fair play and
substantial justice.'" Int'l Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310, 316–17 (1945)
(quoting Milliken v. Meyer, 311 U.S. 457, 463 (1941)).
III. Standard of Review
To survive a motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, a plaintiff bears "the
burden of proving personal jurisdiction over a nonresident" by making "a prima facie
showing of jurisdiction either in the complaint or in affidavits." Cockrell v. Hillerich
& Bradsby Co., 363 S.C. 485, 491, 611 S.E.2d 505, 508 (2005). We must affirm a
trial court's personal jurisdiction ruling unless it has no factual support or was the
result of an error of law. See Atl. Soft Drink Co. of Columbia v. S.C. Nat'l Bank, 287
S.C. 228, 233, 336 S.E.2d 876, 879 (1985).
IV. General and Specific Personal Jurisdiction: The Framework
There are two types of personal jurisdiction: general and specific. A court has
general (or "all purpose") jurisdiction over an individual in the state of his domicile
and over a corporation in its state of incorporation and the state where it has its
principal place of business. Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117, 137 (2014). As
its name implies, general jurisdiction is broad—in most instances, a court that has
general jurisdiction over a defendant may hear cases of any type against that
defendant, regardless of where the conduct occurred or the claim arose.
17

This case turns on specific jurisdiction. A court has specific (or "case-linked")
jurisdiction over a non-resident defendant when the claim has a sufficient connection
to the forum state. The sufficiency of the connection depends upon the relationship
between the defendant, the forum, and the claim. For specific jurisdiction to attach,
three conditions must be met. Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 472–
78 (1985). First, the defendant must have "purposefully avail[ed] itself of the
privilege of conducting activities within the forum state, thus invoking the benefits
and protections of its laws." Hanson v. Denckla, 357 U.S. 235, 253 (1958). The
requisite contacts cannot be random, nor can they be generated by the unilateral
actions of a third party.
Second, the claim must "arise out of or relate to" the defendant's contacts with the
forum state. Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct., 592 U.S. 351, 359
(2021) (quoting Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Ct. of California, San
Francisco Cnty., 582 U.S. 255, 262 (2017)). That is, there must be a link between
the forum and the claims, typically an activity or occurrence that took place in the
forum state. Id. at 359–60.
Third, the exercise of personal jurisdiction over the defendant must comply with the
fundamental fairness that due process guarantees, which International Shoe
expressed as "the traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice."
V. LG's Arguments Against Specific Personal Jurisdiction
LG does not dispute that, by its commercial presence here, it has purposefully
availed itself of doing business in South Carolina markets. It stridently disputes,
however, the second specific jurisdiction requirement: that Fleming's claims arise
out of or relate to LG's South Carolina contacts. LG presses two main arguments.
The first attacks the allegations of Fleming's complaint that LG has distributed or
sold 18650 lithium-ion batteries in South Carolina. The second maintains that
because LG only designs, markets, and sells 18650 batteries in multi-packs to
commercial customers for use as component parts and does not distribute or sell
individual batteries directly to consumers for personal use, Fleming's injury cannot
arise out of or relate to LG's South Carolina contacts.
A. Fleming's Complaint and LG's Distribution of 18650 Batteries in South
Carolina
18

Fleming's complaint states he was injured by an LG lithium-ion battery and LG has
systematically and continuously sold lithium-ion batteries in South Carolina. LG
counters that Fleming has not shown LG's contacts include distribution or sale of the
18650 lithium-ion battery. According to LG, this absence of evidence is evidence
of the absence of the minimum contacts needed to justify jurisdiction. This argument
suffers from the fatal logical fallacy known as an appeal to ignorance. Easily
identified in the wild by its missing logical step, the fallacy is to assume something
is false because it has not been proven true, and vice versa. Mercifully, its lifespan
is brief in most legal contexts because, as here, it conflicts with the applicable burden
of proof.
The hole in LG's logic is its assumption, without proof, that Fleming's description of
LG's lithium-ion battery activity does not encompass 18650 lithium-ion batteries.
Although it attacks Fleming's jurisdictional allegations as overbroad, it does not
deny them. Nowhere does LG deny that it serves the South Carolina market with
lithium-ion batteries, and nowhere does it deny that this includes the 18650 type.
This non-denial did not flip the burden back to Fleming and require him to prove
that which was never denied. Even if Fleming's general grouping of all lithium-ion
batteries left room for some factual dispute about its scope, at the pleading stage we
are obligated to resolve that dispute in favor of Fleming, not LG. See Brown v. Inv.
Mgmt. & Rsch., Inc., 323 S.C. 395, 399, 475 S.E.2d 754, 756 (1996) ("Courts will
take as true the allegations of the nonmoving party and resolve all factual disputes
in its favor." (quoting 5A Charles A. Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal Practice
and Procedure § 1351 (Supp. 1995))).
B. LG and Individual Consumer Use of LG 18650 Batteries
In its second argument attacking relatedness, LG contends it has never designed,
marketed, distributed, or sold lithium-ion 18650 batteries for personal consumer use
anywhere, much less in South Carolina. It filed an affidavit stating it sells them only
to commercial customers in packs for use as component parts and never to individual
consumers for personal use. Therefore, so LG's theory goes, Fleming's injury was
not caused by LG's conduct but by the unilateral actions of rogue sellers who
somehow obtained the packs, broke them open, and sold single batteries to
consumers. Therefore, according to LG, Fleming's claims cannot "arise out of or
relate to" its contacts or activity within South Carolina.
19

LG's argument rests on a causation theory the United States Supreme Court rejected
in Ford. In that case, Ford Motor Company insisted it could not be subject to
personal jurisdiction in a state just because its vehicles caused an injury in that state.
Instead, specific jurisdiction would be proper only in a forum where Ford's conduct
giving rise to the plaintiff's claim occurred, either where the car was sold or where
it was designed and manufactured. Ford urged that the location of the injury
occurred was irrelevant for personal jurisdiction purposes when Ford's conduct that
caused the injury occurred outside of that state.
Rejecting Ford's arguments, the Court emphasized that "[n]one of our precedents has
suggested that only a strict causal relationship between the defendant's in-state
activity and the litigation will do." Ford, 592 U.S. at 362. The court explained that
a defendant's relationship with a forum state may be enough to support specific
jurisdiction even when there is no proof the plaintiff's claim was caused by the
defendant's in-state conduct. Id. Put another way, an injury may arise out of or be
related to a defendant's contacts even though those contacts did not cause the injury.
The distinction the Ford Court draws between causation and relatedness is sublime,
to say the least. It can perhaps be better understood by remembering that the
touchstone of due process in personal jurisdiction is that an out of state defendant
must have "fair warning" that its activity affecting the forum state may subject it to
being held accountable in that state for related conduct. Burger King Corp., 471
U.S. at 471–72. Fair warning may exist even though the occurrence or activity is
not caused by—but nevertheless arises out of or is related to—the defendant's forum
state contacts.
Although the second or relatedness prong of specific jurisdiction does not demand
that the injury would not have happened but for the defendant's in-state conduct, we
must still examine what the level of relatedness must be. It has long been the law
that specific jurisdiction does not lie over a corporation that, although it may have
systematically and continuously conducted activities in the forum state, did nothing
in that state that relates to the plaintiff's claims. Rather, for specific jurisdiction to
attach, there must be some affiliation between the forum and the litigation,
"principally, activity or an occurrence that takes place in the forum state and is
therefore subject to the State's regulation." Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A.
v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915, 919 (2011). This is consistent with the observation in
International Shoe that even single or occasional acts of a corporation in a state
"because of their nature and quality and the circumstances of their commission, may
be deemed sufficient to render the corporation liable to suit." 326 U.S. at 318.
20

We need not dwell on the far end of the relatedness continuum, for the complaint
demonstrates that LG's activity would meet even a strict causation standard. Ford
reaffirmed the principle that specific jurisdiction may be found when a company
"serves a market for a product in the forum state and the product malfunctions there."
Ford, 592 U.S. at 363. The Court did not hedge on this vital point. Its statement
was not limited to or conditioned upon whether the injury was caused by the intended
use of the product.
Applying this principle is enough for us to decide that LG is subject to specific
personal jurisdiction here. Taking, as we must, Fleming's allegations as true that LG
has systematically and continuously served the lithium-ion battery market in South
Carolina (including the 18650 market), there is little doubt that the occurrence—
Fleming's injury—arises out of and is related to LG's activity here. After all, a
corporation's minimum contacts in a forum state "has never been doubted when the
activities of the corporation there have not only been continuous and systematic, but
also give rise to the liabilities sued on." Int'l Shoe, 326 U.S. at 317.
Also, for purposes of due process, where the injury occurred or who was injured is
relevant. The forum state's interest in exercising jurisdiction intensifies if the injury
occurred in that state and the injury is to one of its citizens. This location connection
goes to the due process concern that the state's jurisdiction be reasonable, which
acknowledges that states have a profound interest in the orderly administration of
their laws. These interests do not wane when the injury occurred by an unintended
use of an out of state company's product to a person outside the company's intended
market. For example, if a battery pack had exploded in South Carolina while in the
back of a truck delivering a shipment of batteries to a South Carolina business and
injuring the truck driver and bystanders, LG could hardly argue that the injuries did
not arise out of or relate to its activity in South Carolina because the truck driver and
the bystanders were not intended users of the product. A non-resident defendant
who has raked in profits by exploiting a state's business market with a product may
not escape jurisdiction by claiming the injury arose out of the unintended use of the
product or caused damage to someone other than an intended user. Such a
jurisdictional rule would be as artificial as it is unprecedented and unfair.
At any rate, the complaint alleges LG not only knew about the widespread use of its
individual lithium-ion batteries by consumers in vaping pens, but it also did little to
21

deter such use, even after it knew these uses were resulting in malfunctions causing
grave injury in this state.
Although, without more, "the place of a plaintiff's injury and residence cannot create
a defendant's contact with the forum state," those places "may be relevant in
assessing the link between the defendant's forum contacts and the plaintiff's suit—
including its assertions of who was injured where." Ford, 592 U.S. at 371. Like the
plaintiffs in Ford, here, Fleming "brought suit in the most natural State—based on
an 'affiliation between the forum and the underlying controversy, principally [an]
activity or an occurrence that t[ook] place' there." Id. at 370 (quoting Bristol-Myers
Squibb Co., 582 U.S. at 262).
We are aware that other courts have confronted similar jurisdictional arguments by
LG and other battery manufacturers. Some have found personal jurisdiction exists,
others have not. Compare L.G. Chem America, Inc. v. Morgan, 670 S.W.3d 341,
351 (Tex. 2023) (holding LG's contacts with Texas were enough to satisfy due
process for personal jurisdiction purposes), and Sullivan v. LG Chem, LTD., 79 F.4th
651, 674 (6th Cir. 2023) (holding a Michigan federal district court had personal
jurisdiction over LG), with Yamashita v. LG Chem, Ltd., 62 F.4th 496, 507–09 (9th
Cir. 2023) (finding the plaintiff did not satisfy his burden of proof for personal
jurisdiction and noting LG's contacts with Hawaii were sales of 18650 batteries to
manufacturers, not stand-alone battery sales to individual consumers).
One of the most recent and prominent is B.D. ex rel. Myers v. Samsung Sdi Co., 143
F.4th 757 (7th Cir. 2025). There, the Seventh Circuit held that Indiana could not
exercise specific jurisdiction over Samsung in a case involving an 18650 lithium-ion
battery that exploded in an Indiana resident's pocket and injured him in Indiana. The
Seventh Circuit fashioned a specific jurisdiction test focusing on whether the non-
resident defendant had availed itself of Indiana's forum by delivering its products
into the stream of commerce expecting Indiana consumers would purchase them. At
this level of generality, the test follows World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v, Woodson,
444 U.S. 286 (1980), scrupulously. The Seventh Circuit went on, though, to refine
the test by separating the stream of commerce into two currents, or what it called the
"end-product" stream and the "derivative-product" stream. B.D., 143 F.4th at 767.
The "end-product" stream denoted 18650 battery packs Samsung marketed and sold
as component parts to commercial customers, while the "derivative product" stream
was consisted of individual 18650 batteries third parties had broken off from the
packs and resold to individuals outside of Samsung's intended distribution chain. Id.
22

at 767–69. The Seventh Circuit held that because the plaintiff was injured by the
derivative product, his claim did not arise out of and was not related to Samsung's
Indiana contacts. Id. at 772–73. Therefore, specific jurisdiction over Samsung was
lacking. Id. at 775; see also Ethridge v. Samsung SDI Co., Ltd., 163 F.4th 136, 139
(5th Cir. 2025) (following the Seventh Circuit's approach in Myers); Franceschi v.
LG Chem, Ltd., 580 P.3d 1279, 1284–86 (Nev. 2025) (same).
With much respect, we find this separatist approach—or intended market
approach—too formalistic. International Shoe warned of the folly of focusing on
mechanical or quantitative approaches to personal jurisdiction. 326 U.S. at 319; see
also Burger King Corp., 471 U.S. at 478 ("The Court long ago rejected the notion
that personal jurisdiction might turn on 'mechanical' tests, or on 'conceptualistic . . .
theories of the place of contracting or of performance.'") (citations omitted) (quoting
Int'l Shoe, 326 U.S. at 319; Hoopeston Canning Co. v. Cullen, 318 U.S. 313, 316
(1943)). Perhaps courts could, with their visible pens, sort what the invisible hand
has unsorted in the marketplace. But such an effort would remove adjudication from
the reality of economic markets. Products have ways of finding markets far afield
of those their creators envisioned. When a company learns of such secondary
markets and continues to indirectly supply them, such activity also supplies the
contacts necessary to support personal jurisdiction over the company in lawsuits that
arise out of or are related to that activity.
The intended market approach is just another way to impose a strict causation
requirement on the specific jurisdiction test. This approach in essence says that an
occurrence that takes place in the forum state does not count as a contact by the non-
resident defendant for jurisdictional purposes unless the occurrence was caused by
the intended scope of the non-resident's activity.
In any event, the intended market approach would not help LG here. Fleming has
made a prima facie showing that LG's conduct demonstrates an intent to serve the
South Carolina market for individual 18650 batteries used in vaping devices. LG is
correct that the mere foreseeability that its product may end up in South Carolina is
not enough to justify jurisdiction. Yet, foreseeability can still be relevant, for "the
foreseeability that is critical to due process is not the mere likelihood that a product
will find its way into the forum State. Rather it is that the defendant's conduct and
connection with the forum state are such that he should reasonably anticipate being
haled into court there." World-Wide Volkswagen, 444 U.S. at 287. The Court in
World-Wide Volkswagen further explained:
23

Hence if the sale of a product of a manufacturer or distributor . . . is not
simply an isolated occurrence, but arises from the efforts of the
manufacturer or distributor to serve directly or indirectly, the market
for its product in other States, it is not unreasonable to subject it to suit
in one of those States if its allegedly defective merchandise has there
been the source of injury to its owner or to others. The forum State does
not exceed its powers under the Due Process Clause if it asserts
personal jurisdiction over a corporation that delivers its products into
the stream of commerce with the expectation that they will be
purchased by consumers in the forum State.
Id. at 297–98. We have followed this expression of the stream of commerce theory.
State v. NV Sumatra Tobacco Trading, Co., 379 S.C. 81, 89–91, 666 S.E.2d 218,
222 (2008).
Fleming has made a prima facie showing that LG has placed lithium-ion batteries in
the stream of commerce knowing they will reach South Carolina and be sold
individually to consumers here. He has further shown that LG knows these sales
have caused injury to individual consumers and knows it has been repeatedly sued
in the courts of this state for injuries arising out of such individual use. These
showings suggest LG's intended market in fact includes individuals seeking to buy
lithium-ion batteries for use in vaping devices. They also fortify our conclusion that
LG received ample "fair warning" that it may have to defend itself in South Carolina
courts for its related conduct here.
We are far removed from the situation where the stream of commerce, aided by the
efforts of third parties, has swept the non-resident defendant's product into a forum
without the defendant's knowledge or design. Fleming's allegations demonstrate that
LG has continued to profit from distributing its products while knowing its
distribution stream has been compromised.
In sum, LG's contacts with South Carolina that relate to Fleming's injury are not
random or fortuitous. It does not offend due process to require LG to defend itself
in a forum where it has known its products have been sold and wreaked injury.
c. Fair Play and Substantial Justice
The third and last aspect of specific jurisdiction we must resolve brings us back to
the overarching directive that the non-resident's contacts with the forum state must
24

be extensive enough so that the exercise of jurisdiction is fundamentally fair to LG,
meaning it is consistent with traditional due process notions of fair play and
substantial justice. Chase Secs. Corp. v. Donaldson, 325 U.S. 304, 316–17 (1945).
By its wide operation in the South Carolina lithium-ion battery market, LG benefits
from the protection of our laws that empower LG to defend its property rights,
enforce its contracts, and create the hospitable market in which it has chosen to sell
its lithium-ion batteries. This places a reciprocal obligation on LG to comply with
the laws of that state that regulate its conduct and protect the safety of the state's
citizens. Under such circumstances, it can be neither unfair, unjust, nor surprising
to LG to be subject to suit here to enforce these obligations. And principles of
interstate federalism support allowing jurisdiction here to advance South Carolina's
legitimate interests in enforcing our own laws and providing our resident citizens
with a convenient forum to seek compensation for injuries inflicted on our resident
citizens by non-residents who have conducted significant activity here related to
those injuries.
Finally, allowing LG to evade jurisdiction here would allow it to distribute and sell
goods in the South Carolina market without complying with the same safety laws
and regulations that other companies doing business here must honor.
VI. Conclusion
Because we conclude South Carolina may exert specific personal jurisdiction over
LG in this case, the rulings of the trial court and the court of appeals are
REVERSED.

Hall, concur.

STANDARD OF REVIEW
"Our standard of review in PCR cases depends on the specific issue before us. We
defer to a PCR court's findings of fact and will uphold them if there is evidence in
the record to support them." Smalls v. State, 422 S.C. 174, 180, 810 S.E.2d 836,
839 (2018). "Questions of law are reviewed de novo, and we will reverse the PCR
court's decision when it is controlled by an error of law." Sellner v. State, 416 S.C.
606, 610, 787 S.E.2d 525, 527 (2016).
LAW/ANALYSIS
Petitioner contends the PCR court erred when it determined trial counsel was not
ineffective. The trial court's instruction that "malice does not necessarily mean an
actual intent to kill" almost immediately followed the reading of the statute's "with
intent to kill" language. Petitioner argues these instructions were confusing, and
the jury's questions to the trial court emphasized its confusion. Petitioner asserts
trial counsel was deficient for failing to object to these instructions given this
court's opinion in State v. King.5 Petitioner also argues this deficiency prejudiced
him because testimony revealed he and Wallace were engaged in a struggle at the

"An ineffective assistance claim has two components: A petitioner must show that
counsel's performance was deficient, and that the deficiency prejudiced the
defense." Wiggins v. Smith, 539 U.S. 510, 521 (2003). "[T]he defendant must

reasonableness." Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668, 688 (1984). "Even if a
defendant shows that particular errors of counsel are unreasonable . . . the
defendant must show that they actually had an adverse effect on the defense. It is
not enough for the defendant to show that the errors had some conceivable effect
on the outcome . . . ." Id. at 693. Essentially, the petitioner must show that "but
for counsel's error, there is a reasonable probability the result of the proceedings
would have been different." Boan v. State, 388 S.C. 272, 275-76, 695 S.E.2d 850,
852 (2010). "[T]here is no reason for a court deciding an ineffective assistance
claim to approach the inquiry in the same order or even to address both

Strickland, 466 U.S. at 697.

South Carolina." State v. Lee-Grigg, 374 S.C. 388, 405, 649 S.E.2d 41, 50 (Ct.

presented at trial." Id.
Section 16-3-29 of the South Carolina Code (2015) defines attempted murder: "A
person who, with intent to kill, attempts to kill another person with malice
aforethought, either expressed or implied . . . ." This court clarified that the statute
requires the State to prove specific intent to kill in King I, 412 S.C. at 410, 722
S.E.2d at 193.6 The supreme court affirmed that holding and expanded on this
court's reasoning in 2017. State v. King (King II), 422 S.C. 47, 54-64, 810 S.E.2d

petition for writ of certiorari in King I a week before trial. However, this court's
decision still bound lower courts unless or until the supreme court reversed King I's
holding, and the current and correct law at the time of trial was that attempted
murder required a specific intent to kill. See Hamby v. Hamby, 315 S.C. 518, 520,
445 S.E.2d 656, 657 (Ct. App. 1994) (holding that a court of appeals decision was
applicable in another action even though the supreme court had not yet affirmed
that decision); Perry, 440 S.C. at 406-07, 406 n.11, 892 S.E.2d at 278 & n.11
(citing the holding of King regarding specific intent to kill as binding on the trial
court even though the relevant trial took place between the issuance of King I and
King II); see also In re Kingsmore, 295 B.R. 812, 817 (Bankr. D.S.C. 2002) ("[A]
decision by an intermediate appellate court in South Carolina is the law of South
Carolina unless that decision is subsequently reversed or overruled."). Thus, even
if trial counsel were aware of King I's holding, any belief that the general intent
instruction was proper would have been in anticipation of a change in the law after
the supreme court's review. However, an attorney is "never required to anticipate
or discover changes in the law, or facts which did not exist, at the time of the trial."
Thornes v. State, 310 S.C. 306, 309-10, 426 S.E.2d 764, 765 (1993).
36

Additionally, an attorney is expected to be aware of the currently applicable law in
a client's case. See Hinton v. Alabama, 571 U.S. 263, 274 (2014) ("An attorney's
ignorance of a point of law that is fundamental to his case combined with his
failure to perform basic research on that point is a quintessential example of
unreasonable performance under Strickland."). Trial counsel indicated at the PCR
hearing that he did not have a specific reason for not objecting to either the omitted
instruction on specific intent or the confusing malice charge. Trial counsel's
misapprehension of the holding in King I rendered him unaware of an element of
the offense with which Petitioner was charged. Further, trial counsel twice failed
to object to the trial court's charge that "malice does not necessarily mean an intent
to kill" and also failed to object to the trial court's instruction on general intent.
Failing to object in the face of these instructions on a crime that requires the State
to prove specific intent to kill, or to request instructions on that element, is
deficient performance. See United States v. Freeman, 24 F.4th 320, 326-27, 329
(4th Cir. 2022) (holding that waiver of a meritorious objection when "counsel was
unequivocally wrong on the law" was deficient performance).
Accordingly, the PCR court erred in not determining that trial counsel was
deficient.
II. Prejudice
"Prejudice in ineffective assistance of counsel claims is typically analyzed using a
harmless error framework." Carrier v. State, 441 S.C. 547, 558, 895 S.E.2d 679,
685 (Ct. App. 2023).
"When considering whether an error with respect to a jury instruction was
harmless, we must determine beyond a reasonable doubt that the error complained
of did not contribute to the verdict." Perry, 440 S.C. at 408, 892 S.E.2d at 279
(quoting State v. Burdette, 427 S.C. 490, 496, 832 S.E.2d 575, 578 (2019)). "Jury
instructions must be considered as a whole, and if, as a whole, they are reasonably
free from error, isolated portions which might be misleading do not constitute
reversible error." State v. Kerr, 330 S.C. 132, 144, 498 S.E.2d 212, 218 (Ct. App.
1998). "[O]ur inquiry is not what the verdict would have been had the jury been
given the correct charge, but whether the erroneous charge contributed to the
verdict rendered." Id. at 145, 498 S.E.2d at 218. When a jury is recharged in
response to an inquiry, an appellate court must infer the jury gave "critical
37

attention" to the recharge. State v. Blassingame, 271 S.C. 44, 46-47, 244 S.E.2d
528, 530 (1978).
This court in King I held that an erroneous jury charge instructing that specific
intent to kill was not an element of attempted murder was not harmless error
because the evidence conflicted as to whether the defendant chased the victim or
shot only once during a struggle. 412 S.C. at 417, 772 S.E.2d at 196. The court
held that hearsay testimony from a law enforcement officer that the defendant fired
three to four shots was erroneously admitted. Id. at 411-16, 772 S.E.2d at 193-96.
Considering the evidence presented, the court explained:
[The victim's] testimony that he repeatedly pushed King's
gun away supports the inference that when King shot [the
victim] in the cab, he did so in a struggle and did not
intend to kill [the victim]. It is more difficult to imagine,
however, that King could have chased [the victim] down
Carlton Street while shooting at him unless he
specifically intended to kill . . . .
Therefore, we find [the officer's] inadmissible testimony
as to the number of shots King fired affected the jury's
verdict on attempted murder, and we cannot say that
either the admission of the evidence or the erroneous jury
charge are harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.
Id. at 417, 772 S.E.2d at 196.8
However, our supreme court in Perry affirmed a conviction for attempted murder
even though the trial court recharged the jury on intent using general intent
language referencing "motive" because clear corroborating evidence of specific
intent rendered the erroneous charge harmless. 440 S.C. at 408, 892 S.E.2d at 279.
8 Although this court did not analyze the prejudicial effect of the erroneous charge
alone, the supreme court in King II expanded on this court's specific intent analysis
and concluded, "[W]e agree with the Court of Appeals that the trial judge erred in
charging the jury that a specific intent to kill is not an element of attempted
murder. Further, we agree that this error cannot be deemed harmless." King II,
422 S.C. at 64, 810 S.E.2d at 27 (emphasis added).
38

In that case, the defendant was charged with attempted murder for firing a gun at a
law enforcement officer while fleeing a traffic stop. Id. at 399-400, 892 S.E.2d at
275. The evidence conflicted as to whether the defendant shot into the air or at the
officer. Id. At trial—which also occurred between King I and King II—the jury
requested a recharge on attempted murder and asked additional questions about
malice and the definition of intent. Id. at 401-02, 402 n.5, 892 S.E.2d at 276 & n.5.
In its answer, the trial court mentioned motive and did not clarify the meaning of
specific intent. Id. at 407, 892 S.E.2d at 279. The supreme court held that
mentioning motive confused general and specific intent and failing to be more
precise in defining specific intent was error. Id. However, the court determined
the error was harmless because eyewitness testimony that the defendant shot in the
officer's direction was sufficient evidence of specific intent to prevent finding that
the jury convicted based only on general intent. Id. at 408, 892 S.E.2d at 279.
The supreme court in State v. Smith held that a jury charge on "felony attempted
murder" was not harmless error because it removed the burden on the State to
prove all the elements of attempted murder. 430 S.C. 226, 233, 845 S.E.2d 495,
498 (2020) (per curiam). In that case, rival gang members approached the
defendant, and they exchanged insults before the defendant fired at the group,
missing them and hitting an uninvolved bystander. Id. at 230-31, 845 S.E.2d at
497. The defendant was indicted for attempted murder and four gun charges. Id.
at 231, 845 S.E.2d at 497. At trial, the defendant conceded guilt on two
possession-related gun charges, and the State conceded that the evidence was
sufficient to charge the jury on self-defense. Id. However, the State also requested
the trial court instruct the jury that malice could be inferred when the attempted
murder took place during the commission of a felony. Id. at 231-32, 845 S.E.2d at
497. The trial court gave that instruction on implied malice, which the supreme
court determined was erroneous. Id. at 232, 845 S.E.2d at 497-98. The supreme
court held:
Smith twice conceded guilt to the two felon-in-
possession charges. By requesting the felony attempted-
murder charge after Smith had already conceded guilt to
the predicate felonies, the State essentially eliminated its
own burden to prove all of the elements of attempted
murder beyond a reasonable doubt, specifically that
Smith acted with malice aforethought. For a
constitutional error of this magnitude, "We need go no
39

further than saying we cannot conclude the error was
harmless beyond a reasonable doubt."
Id. at 233, 845 S.E.2d at 498 (quoting State v. Belcher, 385 S.C. 597, 611, 685
S.E.2d 802, 809 (2009)).
The trial court in this case did not instruct the jury on specific intent but did
instruct the jury on malice and general intent. The trial court specifically
instructed that the defendant did not need to have an "actual intent to kill" to have
malice in the original charge and also in response to the jury's questions. Further,
the court read the statute and gave a general criminal intent instruction that
included the statement that criminal intent "may arise from negligence,
recklessness, or indifferen[ce] to duty or to the consequences that is considered by
the law to be the equivalent of criminal intent." At the very least, these instructions
confused general intent and the statute's "with intent to kill" element. Taken as a
whole, the jury instructions describe general intent, and the jury had the option to
convict Petitioner if it found he simply intended to stab defendant with reckless
indifference as to the possibility it may have resulted in Wallace's death. Thus,
similar to the implied malice instruction in Smith, the trial court's jury instructions
essentially eliminated the State's burden to prove Petitioner had a specific intent to
kill Wallace when he stabbed him.
The State argues—and the PCR court determined—that Petitioner conceded he
intended to stab Wallace, and the jury implicitly found his conduct was done with
malice. Thus, the State asserts any error in jury instructions was harmless because
the jury's verdict shows Petitioner intended to stab Wallace with malice and the
specific intent to kill can be inferred.9 See State v. Sutton, 340 SC 393, 397 n.5,
9 We note that the PCR court in its order and the State at the PCR hearing and on
appeal suggest specific intent to kill is satisfied as long as the act itself is

(2) action taken for the purpose of carrying out that intent. See Geter, 445 S.C. at
147-48, 912 S.E.2d at 259 (noting these two elements and malice are the three
elements of attempted murder). Petitioner's conceding he intended to stab Wallace
is dispositive of the latter element only if the State satisfied its burden to prove
Petitioner intended to kill Wallace when stabbing him. The State appears to argue
any error was harmless because the implicit finding by the jury of a malicious,

532 S.E.2d 283, 285 n.5 (2000) ("A specific intent to kill may be, and normally is,
inferred from the surrounding circumstances, such as the character of the attack,
the use of a deadly weapon, and the nature and extent of the victim's injuries."); see
also State v. Taylor, 434 S.C. 365, 370, 862 S.E.2d 924, 927 (Ct. App. 2021)
("[N]othing . . . prevents a jury from being charged that it can look at a defendant's

However, attempted murder requires a higher level of mens rea than the malice
aforethought the jury implicitly found, see King II, 422 S.C. at 56, 810 S.E.2d at 22
("[I]t may seem counterintuitive for the attempt of a crime to require a higher level
of mens rea than that of the completed crime . . . ."), and the evidence does not
clearly indicate a specific intent to kill. Similar to the evidence of a struggle in
King, Petitioner's entire case was predicated on the theory that he did not intend to
kill Wallace when he stabbed him but acted in self-defense to "remove whatever
was happening to him and leave the store." The surrounding circumstances
revealed at trial support this theory. Petitioner and Wallace had a history of
violence and threats between them, Wallace initiated the altercation, Petitioner
always carried his knife and did not bring it to the store for the purpose of fighting,
and the evidence conflicted as to whether Petitioner stabbed Wallace after the fight
separated. Although the jury was not convinced Petitioner's conduct satisfied the
elements of self-defense, the jury could have found Petitioner stabbed Wallace
intending to force Wallace to release him and not intending to cause death.
This case is distinguishable from Perry—in which the supreme court found explicit
evidence of specific intent rendered erroneous instructions harmless—because the
question for the jury in that case was whether the shot fired was accidental or
directed at the pursuing officer. In other words, the issue was largely a factual
dispute and not differing theories about the mental state behind the stipulated
actions of the defendant. Further, the trial court's instruction in Perry simply
mentioned the irrelevant legal principle of motive—a term associated with general
intentional act is equivalent to specific intent to kill. As previously explained, this
construction would essentially eliminate the State's burden to prove the element of
specific intent to kill. See King II, 422 S.C. at 56, 810 S.E.2d at 22-23 (noting
specific intent to kill is a higher level of mens rea than malice). To the extent the
State asserts specific intent to kill can be inferred here, as explained in the
following analysis, we disagree.
41

intent—whereas the court here instructed the jury on general intent only. In fact,
the jury instruction here on malice directly conflicted with the element of specific
intent when the jury was told twice that "malice does not necessarily mean an
actual intent to kill." Thus, this case is closer to the situation in King in which
conflicting evidence was presented as to whether the defendant fired his weapon
during a struggle or while chasing the victim, and the element of specific intent to
kill was directly contradicted in the jury instruction.
Notably, the jury asked to be recharged on the attempted murder statute, asked
what qualifies a person to be convicted of attempted murder, and asked for an
explanation on the difference between premeditation and intent. Thus, the
meaning of attempted murder and intent—and the statement "malice does not
necessarily mean an actual intent to kill"—is presumed to have been given "critical
attention" by the jury. See Blassingame, 271 S.C. at 46-47, 244 S.E.2d at 530.
Given the only specific intent instruction the jury received was the reading of the
statute, we cannot say beyond a reasonable doubt that the erroneous instructions
did not contribute to the jury's verdict when the statute alone "does not clearly
indicate what level of intent the Legislature meant to require." King I, 412 S.C. at
408, 772 S.E.2d at 192.
In sum, we cannot say beyond reasonable doubt that the omission of a specific
intent charge did not contribute to the verdict. By failing to charge the jury on
specific intent to kill, the State's burden of proof was eliminated for an element of
attempted murder, and conflicting evidence prevents an inference of specific intent
to kill. Thus, the error was not harmless, and we reverse the PCR court's
determination that the Petitioner was not prejudiced by the erroneous jury
instructions.
CONCLUSION
The PCR court erred in determining trial counsel's performance was not deficient
as to the trial court's incorrect jury instructions on intent for the crime of attempted
murder and in determining Petitioner was not prejudiced by that performance.
Accordingly, we reverse the PCR court's denial of Petitioner's application for PCR
due to ineffective assistance of counsel.
